issues.explanation: The trigger 'Arab villages' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of physical abuse by a romantic partner and the rest of the profile, which centers on interpersonal abuse-related cues, self-appraisals, and memory phenomena. Without any corresponding threat, memory, or appraisal content involving war, military, or ethnic/geographic conflict, this item appears clinically incoherent for this patient.

issues.item: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Strictly restricting eating to feel in control is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other selected items coherently describe PTSD related to partner physical abuse (criticism, violence, offender cues; fragmented/alien memory; rage; dehumanization, self-blame, emotional numbing; distraction and cue avoidance). In contrast, restrictive eating introduces a distinct control-focused coping pattern that is not reflected elsewhere in triggers, memory, threat, or appraisals, making it clinically hard to explain as part of the same formulation rather than a separate problem.

vignette: Tane was seventy-four now, but the memory of Marcus’s hands on his throat decades ago still sat cold in his chest. He had met his partner at a community gathering in Honolulu, drawn to a man who initially seemed steady, only to find himself trapped in a house where correction was met with escalating violence. When Tane questioned a budget discrepancy or simply hesitated to comply, Marcus would corner him, his grip bruising the ribs, his breath hot and threatening. The abuse was a slow suffocation; Marcus would destroy Tane’s property and then demand he apologize for provoking the assault. Over time, Tane came to believe he was fundamentally character-flawed, convinced the event happened to him because of the sort of person he is. This conviction warped how his mind archived the trauma, ensuring he remembered the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in his mind, devoid of contextual flow. When he spotted a man who resembled Marcus in a crowded grocery aisle, or when a client’s sharp email demanded yet another revision, the sight would instantly flash back to the bruised knuckles of those nights, and the sudden spike would force him to immediately close his laptop and scroll aimlessly through news sites, deliberately pulling his attention away from the screen. His relentless habit of blocking out strong sensations and sidestepping any reminder of the person who harmed him only ensured that the unprocessed memories continued to intrude as unbidden fragments. He had systematically purged his home of anything that might remind him of his ex-partner and refused to allow himself to feel any strong emotion, convincing himself that detachment was the only way to survive. But his emotional numbness and constant deflection slowly convinced him that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, cementing his belief that he felt like an object, not like a person. When those frozen snapshots of Marcus’s raised arm surfaced, intense rage would flood his chest, making it impossible to sit still, so he would immediately stand and pace the room, forcing himself to avoid letting any strong feeling settle. The lingering fear from those intrusions would bleed back into his daily routine, making ordinary corrections feel dangerously alive so that every red pen mark would instantly reactivate his alertness to potential violence. The more he avoided those triggers and numbed his own reactions, the more hypersensitive his nerves became, until even a minor critique would detonate his fear of sudden violence. At seventy-four, Tane finally booked a consultation with a trauma clinic after a panic attack during a routine copy-editing session left him unable to speak for hours. He hoped to quiet the rage before it consumed him, terrified that the critic’s voice would always be the prelude to violence, and that he would never again feel like a real man. He spent his evenings staring at the city lights from behind drawn blinds, waiting for a numbness that would not come, knowing that his own mind had become a cage of his worst fears.
